reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that studentized bootstrap intervals correct for skewness through second-order Edgeworth expansions, which align with Cornish-Fisher quantile corrections. In contrast, percentile-based intervals fail under skewness due to first-order approximation errors. The asymmetric nature of t* under right-skewed data arises from the inversion of tails—whereby the upper tail extends further than the lower. This asymmetry is captured in the studentized pivot formulation, where t* = (x̄ − θ)/SE(x̄), and the empirical distribution of t* deviates from symmetry. The coverage ordering reflects this: studentized intervals dominate BCa, which dominates percentile, because they incorporate higher-order corrections. The jackknife SE provides an exact formula for standard error under the mean, enabling faster computation without sacrificing accuracy. These primitives form a kernel of robust uncertainty quantification under non-normality, especially in small samples.
